case_prompt: A 34-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 5-day history of bitemporal headache and 24 hours of intense, throbbing, continuous left neck pain radiating to the ipsilateral mandibular and auricular region. The pain was localized over the left carotid bifurcation and worsened with neck movement and palpation. Physical and neurologic examinations were normal. He denied trauma, recent infection, or chiropractic manipulation; his medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, coagulation tests, electrolytes, glucose, renal and liver function tests—were within normal limits. The white-cell count was 7 g/L (reference, 4–10 g/L), C-reactive protein was 6.3 mg/L (reference, 0–10 mg/L), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was mildly elevated at 11 mm/h (reference, 0–10 mm/h). Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed soft-tissue thickening around the distal common carotid artery, the carotid bulb, and the proximal internal carotid artery on the left, with no abnormalities of other supra-aortic vessels or the aortic arch. Doppler ultrasonography showed an isoechoic thickened arterial wall at the left carotid bifurcation, a peak systolic velocity of 90 cm/s, normal intraluminal flow, and “No intimal dissection or aneurysm was seen.” MRI of the neck demonstrated eccentric soft-tissue thickening at the left carotid bifurcation with a hypointense T1 signal, hyperintense T2 signal, no T1 wall hematoma on fat-saturated sequences, and intense perivascular enhancement after contrast administration. Serologic testing was negative, with “negative immunological laboratory tests including anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) and antinuclear antibodies (ANA).” An abdominal MRI showed “no vascular abnormality (no fibromuscular dysplasia, no vasculitis, and no stenosis).”

sentences.text: A 34-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 5-day history of bitemporal headache and 24 hours of intense, throbbing, continuous left neck pain radiating to the ipsilateral mandibular and auricular region.
The pain was localized over the left carotid bifurcation and worsened with neck movement and palpation.
Physical and neurologic examinations were normal. He denied trauma, recent infection, or chiropractic manipulation; his medical history was otherwise unremarkable.
Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, coagulation tests, electrolytes, glucose, renal and liver function tests—were within normal limits.
The white-cell count was 7 g/L (reference, 4–10 g/L), C-reactive protein was 6.3 mg/L (reference, 0–10 mg/L), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was mildly elevated at 11 mm/h (reference, 0–10 mm/h).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed soft-tissue thickening around the distal common carotid artery, the carotid bulb, and the proximal internal carotid artery on the left, with no abnormalities of other supra-aortic vessels or the aortic arch.

Doppler ultrasonography showed an isoechoic thickened arterial wall at the left carotid bifurcation, a peak systolic velocity of 90 cm/s, normal intraluminal flow, and “No intimal dissection or aneurysm was seen.” MRI of the neck demonstrated eccentric soft-tissue thickening at the left carotid bifurcation with a hypointense T1 signal, hyperintense T2 signal, no T1 wall hematoma on fat-saturated sequences, and intense perivascular enhancement after contrast administration.

Serologic testing was negative, with “negative immunological laboratory tests including anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) and antinuclear antibodies (ANA).” An abdominal MRI showed “no vascular abnormality (no fibromuscular dysplasia, no vasculitis, and no stenosis).”

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Large‐vessel arteritis was considered but deemed unlikely — “In large vessel arteritis (giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis), the thickened arterial wall enhances intensively on MRI; however, this enhancement is generally associated with significant luminal stenosis and it is not limited to the carotid bifurcation.” 2. Fibromuscular dysplasia was ruled out — abdominal MRI showed “no vascular abnormality (no fibromuscular dysplasia, no vasculitis, and no stenosis).” 3. Arteriosclerosis was unlikely — “No pathology of the other supra‐aortic arteries or of the aortic cross was found.” 4. Aneurysm was excluded — “No intimal dissection or aneurysm was seen.” 5. Systemic vasculitis was ruled out — “negative immunological laboratory tests including anti‐neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) and antinuclear antibodies (ANA).”

selection.screen_reason: Acute focal pain over the carotid bifurcation with perivascular soft-tissue thickening and no dissection, stenosis or vasculitis gives idiopathic carotidynia.
selection.second_look_note: Focal throbbing pain over the carotid bifurcation without trauma or manipulation frames the problem; neck imaging excluding dissection and vasculitis decides.
